title: Tourists, residents, and chickens in urban spaces: the case of Ybor City
setting: street (Ybor City, Tampa, Florida - historic entertainment district defined for the study as eleven-by-six city blocks: the 7th Avenue commercial corridor, residential side streets, rail bank, pocket parks and Centennial Park weekend market)
design: qualitative (author calls it a mixed method approach: a one-day on-foot mapping survey of chicken sightings and audible rooster crowing along a predetermined route covering the whole neighbourhood, 12:50-14:30 on a midweek January afternoon 2020, plus three further site visits; 1-2 minute oral 'flash interviews' with visitors; and six semi-structured key-informant interviews, five by Zoom)
sample_n: 21 flash-interview respondents (19 visitors - 7 greater Tampa, 2 elsewhere in Florida, 10 out-of-state - and 2 people working in Ybor City) + 6 key informants (planning officials, residents/neighbourhood activists, tourism professionals, a bird-behaviour biologist) (analytic unit for the maps: 56 chicken sightings and 56 audible rooster-crowing events)
exposure: Feral rooster crowing as a component of the neighbourhood soundscape, mapped by the author walking the whole neighbourhood 'equipped with normal vision and hearing' and recording every location where crowing was audible (Methods [page 9]; Fig. 3 sound map [page 11]); crowing occurred on average once every second minute and carried approximately one urban block, while on 7th Avenue 'the sounds of people, cars, and music typically drowns out the sound of roosters' ([page 13]). Reverse exposure: user and business behaviour that shapes this soundscape - tourists and shops buying and distributing chicken feed, restaurants leaving bread out and dumpster waste drawing birds toward the commercial core, people from elsewhere dropping off unwanted backyard roosters which skews the rooster-to-hen ratio and 'result[s] in an increase in rooster crowing' ([pages 5-6, 12-13, 16]), and rising pedestrian/vehicular traffic after which 'chickens later retreat to calmer neighborhood spaces' ([page 13]). No sound level measurement: 'What amounts to noise pollution is not just a matter of decibel levels, but the character of sounds' ([page 16])
behaviour_measure: Locations of human-chicken encounters and the 'common chicken-human contact zone' derived from the sighting and crowing maps (daytime visitors exploring side streets, entering/leaving parking facilities, visiting the weekend market, [page 13-14]); reported visitor behaviours of engaging with and feeding chickens in the streets and buying chicken feed, and businesses leaving out bread ([pages 12-13]); reported coping behaviours of residents and short-term-rental hosts (keeping windows closed, guest complaints, informal 'rehoming' of large numbers of chickens to farms, fencing flower beds, 'Please Don't Feed the Chickens' signage) ([pages 6, 12, 16-17]). No counts or rates of human behaviour were recorded
measurement_method: observation (author's pedestrian mapping survey of chicken sightings and audible crowing plus in-situ observation over three further visits); self-report (21 flash interviews and 6 key-informant interviews, recorded in hand-written field notes)
key_finding: Sound was as pervasive as sight: 56 audible crowing events matched 56 chicken sightings, so 'a person is about as likely to hear as to see chickens', with crowing about once every second minute and audible roughly one block ([page 13]). Human activity shaped that soundscape - traffic, people and music mask crowing on 7th Avenue, chickens withdraw from the corridor as pedestrian and vehicular traffic increases, and feeding by tourists and businesses plus dumping of unwanted roosters concentrate birds (and crowing) nearer the commercial core, so the human-chicken contact zone is the side streets, parking facilities and weekend market. Visitors were unanimously positive and valued the aural element as part of the neighbourhood's authenticity and ambiance ('I like to hear them crowing'; 'I love the feel of it'), and no visitor expressed a negative view, which the author attributes to visitors not being woken by crowing. Residents were split: unpredictable 3-4 a.m. crowing is the leading anti-chicken argument and prompted closed windows, Airbnb guest complaints and informal removal of birds
effect_stats: NR (qualitative, descriptive counts only): 56 chicken sightings and 56 audible rooster-crowing events recorded over a 1 h 40 min walk (12:50-14:30), 'Fifty-six "crowing events" were detected, which is identical to the 56 chicken sightings ... with an average, according to the data, once every second minute. The sound of a rooster carries approximately one urban block' ([page 13]); 21 flash interviews and 6 key-informant interviews ([pages 9-10]); no statistical tests, no sound level measurements
